cycles.name: Bedrock
focuses: Rebuild the brace and posterior chain with trunk-supported hinging — no loaded free hinge, low back stays quiet.
Heavy upper-back and scapular bias aimed straight at fixing the posture — pulling beats pressing this block.

paragraphs: Welcome, Faraz. This first block is about building your base back up before we load anything heavy. Your back has a long history, so we're not jumping straight into squats and deadlifts. Everything here is picked so your back stays quiet while the rest of you gets stronger.

The main job is your upper back. That rounded posture you want to fix doesn't come from stretching, it comes from getting the muscles between your shoulder blades strong enough to hold you up. So you'll pull a lot more than you push in these four weeks.
Keep every set at 7 out of 10 effort, no more. You should leave the gym feeling like you had a bit left. That's on purpose, not me going easy on you.
outcomes: Back stays pain-free for the full 4 weeks
Leg press and hip thrust moving up every week
Real numbers on the board to build cycle 2 from

cycles.name: Rigging
focuses: Hypertrophy-bias upper back and posterior chain — rows, pulls, rear delts — the engine of the tone and posture goal.
The hinge graduates: light dumbbell RDL grooved at RPE 7 or under while the hip thrust still carries the load.

paragraphs: Block two is where your upper back starts working properly. More pulling, heavier, and you'll actually feel the muscles that hold your posture doing their job.
And if your back stays quiet through these four weeks, the squat comes back. That's the deal I'm making with you.
Give me one quiet month and the bar is yours.

cycles.name: Keystone
focuses: First real strength push — barbell RDL enters at conservative loads, squat and press build toward RPE 8 top sets.
Upper-back volume held as the standing posture floor; the week gets a sharper load identity — one peak, one moderate, one low day.

cycles.name: Rebuild & Reset
focuses: Planned back-off — volume down roughly 40%, every RPE capped at 7, more movement variety so it reads as a new program, not a punishment.
Posture consolidation and an honest check-in on sleep and stress before the heaviest block is allowed to start.

cycles.name: Ironworks
focuses: The heaviest block of the roadmap — top-set and back-off work on squat, hinge and press at RPE 7–8.
Accessories cut to the minimum effective dose so the recovery budget goes to the bar.

cycles.name: Silhouette
focuses: Hypertrophy finishing block biased to upper back, shoulders and arms — the visible shape payoff.
Strength held on low-dose heavy anchors; closes with a posture re-check and the next-arc decision.

cards.title: Your stress is the real limit
cards.body:
You told me stress is a 9 out of 10 and your sleep quality is a 5. That's the number I built this whole block around, not your training experience.

When you sleep badly and life is heavy, your body can't recover from hard training the same way. So the effort stays at 7 out of 10 and the sessions stay short. This isn't me being careful for no reason, it's the fastest way forward for someone with your week.

On a bad day, take 1 off every effort target. If it says 7, do 6. Anything already at 6 stays at 6. You'll still get the benefit.

cards.title: Your back: what's ok, what's not
cards.body:
Your lower back gave you problems for years and it's quiet now. I want to keep it that way, so here's how to read it in the gym.

Normal and fine: muscle burn, being tired, feeling stiff the next morning. Keep training through all of that.

Not fine: sharp pain, anything shooting down your leg, numbness or pins and needles, or pain that gets worse with every rep instead of staying the same.

  • Mild and it fades: finish the set, write it in your log.
  • Building up, or it changes how you move: stop that exercise, use the swap on the card, message me.
  • Sharp, shooting, numb, or just feels wrong: stop the session and message me before the next one.

Messaging me early is never overreacting. It's the whole point of having a coach.

cards.title: How to pick your weights
cards.body:
I don't give you a weight to lift. You find it yourself, and here's how that works.

On a new exercise, start too light on purpose. Do your first set, then ask how hard that was out of 10. If it was a 5, go up next set. If it was an 8 or 9, come down. By your second week you'll know your numbers.

Week to week: if you hit all your reps and it felt like a 7 or easier, put a little more on next week. If you missed reps or it felt like a 9, stay on the same weight and do it again. Repeating a weight is not standing still, it's how it's supposed to go.

Going down is not failing. Bad sleep, stressful week, back feels tight, take weight off. I'd much rather see that in your log than see you grind through something.

cards.title: Why rows fix your posture
cards.body:
You asked me to fix the hunch in your upper back. I want you to know what's actually doing that job, because it's not the stretching.

It's the rows and the pulldowns. Rounded shoulders happen when the muscles across your upper back are too weak to hold you upright all day. Stretching gives you 20 minutes of feeling better. Getting those muscles strong changes how you stand when you're not thinking about it.

That's why you pull about twice as much as you press in this block, and why there's almost no chest work. The short shoulder blade drills in your warm up matter too, don't skip them to save time.

Be patient with this one. Real posture change takes months, not weeks. You should feel a bit taller by week 4, and that's just the start.

cards.title: You already did the hard part
cards.body:
You lost 9kg and you've held it for 20 days. I don't want that to go unmentioned, because keeping weight off is genuinely harder than losing it and most people don't manage it.

You also did it during a rough patch, which makes it more impressive, not less. That's a stable base to build from now.

From here the scale is not something we chase. We're building, not shrinking.

cards.title: Eat to build, not to cut
cards.body:
You said your food is mostly on track, so I'm not changing anything yet. One thing though.

Don't try to keep losing weight during this block. You're asking your body to build muscle and recover on 5 out of 10 sleep and a stressful week. Cutting food on top of that is how people get tired, weak and injured.

Eat normally, get protein at every meal, and let training do the shape change. We'll look at your food properly at the end of the block once I can see how you're recovering.

cards.title: Three days, and the promise
cards.body:
Three sessions a week, in any order that fits your week. If Tuesday falls apart, move it. Nothing here depends on the exact days.

Day 3 is your safety net. On a brutal week, do the back extension and the pulldown and leave. That's 15 minutes and it still counts as a session. Two sessions done properly beats three you skipped because you didn't have time for all of them.

And log every set, even the bad ones. Your log is the only way I can see how you're doing. An honest bad week tells me more than a perfect looking one.

cards.title: You'll want to go heavier. Don't.
cards.body:
You coached tennis for 10 years, so you know how to move and you'll pick these exercises up fast. That's an advantage. It's also the thing most likely to get you in trouble in the next four weeks.

You're going to feel like the weights are too light. Especially in weeks 1 and 2. That's the design, not a mistake. I'm using this block to see how your back and your recovery handle regular training before we put real load on you.

Do it my way for four quiet weeks and cycle 2 gets a lot more interesting.
